venues.d: The city's grandest address — a tree-lined boulevard house with Taipei's most spacious rooms and its most sought-after afternoon tea.
André Fu's 'modern mansion' — 86 rooms of quiet, residential grandeur along a European-style boulevard, opened 2025.
A stalwart of well-heeled Taipei since 1990 — grand, dependable, with its own boutique galleria beneath it.
The first international house in the city, freshly renovated — and the closest grand hotel to Taipei 101.

venues.n: Shangri-La's Far Eastern Plaza Hotel, Taipei
venues.d: The tallest hotel in the city, after a US$50 million refresh — sweeping views and nine restaurants and bars.
The bright, high-energy beacon of the Xinyi business district — the largest luxury hotel in the city.
A design-led boutique house in leafy Da'an — intimate, culinary-minded, and quietly cool.
A large, polished house near the Miramar district — one of the city's best hotel pools and a strong all-round base.
An East-meets-West palace of imported French furniture and antiques — home to the city's three-star Le Palais.
Taipei's crown — Cantonese seafood and dim sum at the highest level, three stars for the eighth year running.
Chef Kai Ho's 'taste of terroir' — modern Taiwanese cooking that put the island's fine dining on the world map.
The late master's counter-dining concept in Taipei — precise French cooking around the famous red-and-black bar.
Ryogo Tahara's cross-Asian tasting menu down a Da'an alley — named the best restaurant in Taiwan.
A rare two-star Spanish kitchen in Asia — an offshoot of the Navarran original, deeply seasonal and precise.
An exacting tempura counter of great purity — the ingredient, the oil, the moment, and nothing else.
Chef Alain Huang's personal French-Taiwanese cooking — promoted to two stars in 2025.
A refined Japanese counter that climbed to two stars in 2025 — quiet, exacting, seasonal.
A meticulous Japanese kitchen newly raised to two stars — kappo cooking with real finesse.
The three-Michelin-star German chef's Taipei room, high in the city — European fine dining, newly starred.
Refined Hangzhou cuisine of long standing — one of Taipei's most gracious classical tables.
The refined face of home-style Taiwanese cooking — heritage recipes served with quiet polish.
Elegant Cantonese cooking inside the Mandarin Oriental — assured, classical, beautifully served.
An intimate Edomae sushi counter newly awarded a star in 2025 — clean, exacting omakase.
Refined contemporary Italian cooking, freshly starred — a warm, ingredient-led kitchen.
A restored old mansion serving classic Taiwanese banquet cooking — recognised for its sustainable sourcing.
The world's most famous dumpling house, born on Taipei's Xinyi Road in 1972 — xiao long bao at their source.
Plant-based Taiwanese whole-food cooking, elevated with delicate Asian flavour — a new Bib Gourmand in 2025.

Ride one of the world's fastest passenger elevators to the 89th-floor observatory, then look down on the 660-tonne golden tuned-mass damper that keeps the tower steady through typhoons and quakes. The 91st-floor outdoor deck is the family photograph; a private guide can pre-book timed entry so multi-gen groups skip the queue entirely.

The tower's lower floors hold a serene luxury mall — the maisons, plus a basement food hall — and the branch of Din Tai Fung that many visitors combine with the observatory. Dumplings and shopping under one roof make an easy, air-conditioned afternoon when the family wants low effort and high polish.

One of the world's greatest collections of Chinese art — jade, bronzes, ceramics, painting and calligraphy carried from Beijing's Forbidden City in 1949. Come at opening on a weekday and take a private art-historian guide; with nearly 700,000 objects rotated in cycles, a curated two-hour route through the masterpieces is far richer than wandering.

A vast white-and-blue marble hall rising above formal gardens and the grand Liberty Square gateway, guarded by soldiers whose hourly changing-of-the-guard drill is a precise, photogenic ceremony. The flanking National Theater and Concert Hall make it a serene early-morning walk before the day's heat.

Taipei's most atmospheric working temple, founded in 1738 in the old Bangka quarter, thick with incense and the murmur of worshippers folding Taoist, Buddhist and folk deities into one courtyard. Visit at dusk when the lanterns glow and locals come to pray; a guide unlocks the etiquette and the meaning behind the offerings.

A jewel of Taiwanese temple craftsmanship dedicated to the God of Medicine, its 19th-century woodcarving, stone dragons and door-god murals painstakingly restored to international acclaim. Quieter than Longshan and paired naturally with the Confucius Temple next door for a calm morning in old Taipei.

A restrained, elegant Confucian temple built in the southern Fujian style, its unadorned dignity a deliberate contrast to the exuberance of Bao'an across the lane. Interactive halls explain the rites and the imperial examination system; the autumn Confucius birthday ceremony with its ancient music and dance is the moment to aim for.

Taipei's largest and most famous night market — a maze of stalls turning out oyster omelettes, pepper buns, giant fried chicken and shaved ice, plus a basement food court. Best experienced with a local guide who can navigate the veg-friendly and Buddhist-vegetarian stalls (Taiwan's meat-free scene is deep) and steer the family to the good vendors.

A tighter, more walkable single-lane market anchored by the Ciyou Temple at one end and famous for its black-pepper pork buns baked in a clay oven. Many food-lovers prefer it to Shilin for its density and lower chaos — an easy evening after a day in the east of the city.

A compact, old-Taipei night market beloved for classic Taiwanese street food — taro balls, egg yolk taro, oyster omelette — with less of the crush of Shilin. It sits at the edge of Dadaocheng, so pair it with an afternoon on Dihua Street for a full old-town day into night.

Taipei's oldest commercial street, a corridor of restored merchant shophouses trading in Chinese medicinal herbs, dried seafood, fabrics and fine Taiwanese tea since the 19th century. A tea master or private guide turns a stroll into a proper tasting and a lesson in the old town's history; it comes alive further at Lunar New Year.

A tiny, jewel-box temple on Dihua Street packed with over six hundred deities — including Yue Lao, the God of Love, which draws pilgrims across Taiwan praying for marriage and relationships. Small enough for a fifteen-minute visit, rich enough to anchor a Dadaocheng walk.

A steaming, sulphur-green geothermal lake — one of the hottest springs feeding all of Beitou — wreathed in mineral vapour and ringed by a short lakeside path. Free to enter and the natural starting point for a hot-spring day in Taipei's thermal quarter.

Taipei's thermal valley is lined with hot-spring hotels where families can book a private in-room or reserved bath rather than share a public pool — the discreet choice for multi-gen groups. The waters run from milky white sulphur to rare radium-bearing green springs; ask the concierge to arrange a private thermal suite.

A graceful 1913 brick-and-timber Japanese bathhouse — once the largest in East Asia — with its grand tiled soaking hall preserved intact and a tatami resting room upstairs. A gentle, free introduction to the town's spa heritage, a short walk from the Thermal Valley.

A quietly beautiful timber library set in Beitou Park, all deep balconies and vertical wooden louvres, and a landmark of green design. A five-minute detour on the hot-spring circuit that architecture-minded travellers genuinely enjoy.

A volcanic upland of steaming fumaroles, sulphur vents, grasslands and — in spring — cherry blossom and calla-lily fields, all within an hour of the city. A private car and driver make it an easy half-day escape from the heat; the Xiaoyoukeng vents and Qingtiangang meadow are the set-pieces.

A short but steep stair-climb of about 20–30 minutes delivers the postcard view of Taipei 101 rising over the city, best at golden hour and into the blue-hour lights. It's the classic city hike; go with a guide who knows the quieter viewing rocks so the family isn't jostling for the shot.

A cable-car glide over forested tea hills to Maokong, where hillside tea houses serve locally grown Tieguanyin with the Taipei skyline below. Book the glass-floored Crystal Cabin for the drama, then settle into a teahouse for an unhurried afternoon — a serene, low-effort day the whole family enjoys.

One of Asia's largest zoos and the lower station of the Maokong Gondola, home to giant pandas and a well-regarded Formosan-animal area. Genuinely engaging for younger members of a multi-gen group and easily combined with the gondola ride above it.

A converted 1914 wine-and-camphor factory now given over to design shops, galleries, indie cinema and rotating art-and-immersive exhibitions, with good cafes in the old brick halls. The most central of Taipei's creative parks — an easy, stylish afternoon between sights.

A former 1937 tobacco factory reborn as a design campus around a tranquil reflecting pool, home to the Taiwan Design Museum and the striking Eslite Spectrum flagship. Calmer and greener than Huashan, and a short walk from Taipei 101.

A monumental hall honouring the founding father of the Republic, with its own hourly military honour-guard ceremony and, from the plaza, one of the cleanest framed views of Taipei 101. The surrounding park is a favourite for morning tai-chi and evening strolls.

venues.n: Miramar Entertainment Park Ferris Wheel (Taipei Eye)
venues.d: A rooftop Ferris wheel atop the Miramar mall in the Dazhi district, lit up at night with a gentle turn over the city and the Keelung River. A relaxed evening spin, easy to pair with dinner in the mall — pleasant for children and grandparents alike.

The end of the red MRT line opens onto a breezy riverside promenade and a food-street of iron-egg, A-gei and fishball snacks, with Taiwan's most celebrated sunset over the Tamsui estuary. An easy half-day that ends with the Fisherman's Wharf Lover's Bridge lit against the dusk.

A red-brick fort begun by the Spanish in 1628, rebuilt by the Dutch and later leased as the British Consulate — a layered relic of Taiwan's colonial trade history above the Tamsui river. The former consular residence and its gardens make it more than a quick fort stop; combine with Tamsui Old Street.

A striking 1908 octagonal red-brick market hall, now a heritage arts-and-crafts venue with a designers' market and a lively creative-district plaza behind it. A quick, characterful stop at the heart of the Ximending shopping quarter.

Taipei's neon pedestrian shopping district — the city's youthful pulse of street fashion, snack stalls, cinemas and buskers, often called its Harajuku. Best after dark; a lively, easy evening for teenagers in the group, with the Red House at its edge.

Taipei's largest central park — a green lung of banyan groves, an egret-filled ecological pond and open lawns, ringed by the city's most walkable cafe-and-boutique neighbourhood. The place to slow down between sights; the surrounding Da'an lanes reward an unhurried wander.

Taiwan's leading contemporary-art museum, set in a handsome 1920s red-brick former city hall and city school, with sharp rotating shows of local and international work. Compact and central — a good hour for collectors and art-minded travellers.

Taiwan's oldest museum, in a neoclassical hall inside the leafy 228 Peace Memorial Park, covering the island's natural history and indigenous cultures. A gentle, air-conditioned stop near the station, good for a mixed-age group on a hot afternoon.

A restored Qing-and-Japanese-era street of arcaded shophouses beside Longshan Temple, its weathered brick facades a favourite film-set and a window into old Bangka life. Free, quick and photogenic — the natural companion to a Longshan Temple visit.

venues.n: Xiangshan / Xinyi rooftop bars & city views
venues.d: The Xinyi district around Taipei 101 holds the city's best sky-high lounges and hotel bars, where a discreet dinner or nightcap comes with the tower framed at eye level. The refined evening counterpart to the daytime observatory — ask the concierge to secure a window table.

A leafy lane synonymous with Taipei eating — beef noodles, mango shaved ice, the original Din Tai Fung nearby, and no end of tea and dessert houses. A stroll-and-graze afternoon; with a food guide it becomes a curated tasting through the city's signature dishes, veg options included.

Taiwan is the birthplace of bubble (boba) tea, and Taipei is where to taste it at its source alongside serious high-mountain oolong and Tieguanyin. A private tea-house session — in Maokong, Dadaocheng or a Da'an salon — is a calm, sensory ritual that suits every generation.

venues.n: Xiaolongbao & the Din Tai Fung story
venues.d: The soup dumpling reached global fame from Din Tai Fung's original Xinyi Road shop — the pleated, 18-fold xiaolongbao is Taipei's edible signature. The Xinyi branch carries a Michelin Bib Gourmand; book ahead or let a guide manage the timing so the family isn't queuing.

A former gold-mining town of lantern-lit stone stairways and cliffside tea houses looking out to the Pacific, its misty lanes widely linked to the mood of Miyazaki's Spirited Away. Go with a private driver and arrive before the crowds; a teahouse balcony at dusk is the moment to hold.

In the old railway town of Shifen you write wishes on a paper sky lantern and release it to drift over the valley — one of Taiwan's most cherished rituals — with the wide Shifen Waterfall a short walk on. A private tour pairs it neatly with Jiufen for a full northern-hills day.

A dramatic coastal cape of wind-and-sea-carved sandstone — the famous 'Queen's Head', mushroom rocks and sea candles strung along a north-coast headland. A striking, easy walk that combines with Jiufen and Shifen on a private northern day trip.

An indigenous Atayal mountain village south of the city with riverside hot springs, a plunging waterfall reached by a little scenic train, and a gondola to a forest plateau. A greener, quieter thermal alternative to Beitou — a restful half-day with a driver.

A working harbour city half an hour north, famed for the buzzing Miaokou Night Market and the wave-sculpted rock coast of Heping Island Park. A good add-on to a north-coast day, or a seafood-focused evening out of the city.

A former coal-mining hamlet on the Pingxi line reborn as a hillside village of resident cats, old railway relics and easy trails. A light, charming stop that slots into a Jiufen–Shifen railway day, especially with children in the group.

A calm central park built around the memorial to the 1947 February 28 Incident, with a small museum that gives sober, essential context to modern Taiwan. A short, meaningful stop that deepens any first visit; it also holds the National Taiwan Museum.

One of Taiwan's finest surviving classical Chinese gardens and merchant mansions, all moon gates, pavilions and reflecting ponds built by the 19th-century Lin family. A serene, cultured half-day for those who love garden architecture, away from the tourist core.

Beside Jiufen, this restored Japanese-era gold-mining settlement lets you walk a real mine tunnel and lift a colossal gold ingot at the Gold Museum, set among quiet mountain temples. The substantive, less-crowded counterpart to touristy Jiufen next door.

Taipei's riverside parks link into hundreds of kilometres of flat, protected bike paths, with Dadaocheng Wharf offering sunset river views, container-bar dining and evening cruises. A relaxed, active way to see the city's water side; bikes and a guide are easily arranged.
A refined, ingredient-led cocktail bar — one of the city's most decorated rooms on the Asian stage.
An experimental, technique-driven bar pushing Taipei's cocktail scene forward — the city's highest-ranked bar of the year.
The bar that built Taipei's cocktail reputation — Aki Wang's tea-and-terroir mixing, a fixture of Asia's best for a decade.
Angus Zou's cocktails-on-tap concept — 'no garnish, no bullshit', casual and fast, and quietly revolutionary.
A minimalist, concept-led bar that earned its place among Asia's best — spare, considered, precise.
The intimate downstairs counter from the Lab team — a more personal, experimental drinking room.
